title: Party identity shifts at the edges while gender, race, and education keep the coalition lines uneven
source_unit: Pew Research Center National Public Opinion Reference Survey (NPORS), 2020-2026 partisan-affiliation fact sheet

self_identified_independent_or_something.unit: percent of U.S. adults before leaners are assigned

observations.method: Pew's multimode, address-based NPORS estimates partisan identification and party leaning across 2020-2026; Republicans and Democrats in the combined measures include leaners.
observations.uncertainty: The data are repeated cross-sectional surveys, not a panel following the same people. Partisan identification is not a vote, ideological position, policy preference, turnout, or durable identity, and the 2026 field period may reflect the political context at that time.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, with comparisons by gender, race and ethnicity, education, age, and birth cohort; Asian estimates are representative of English speakers and some subgroup samples are smaller.
observations.counterinterpretation: A small national party-affiliation shift can reflect sampling, response, political context, or movement among leaners rather than durable coalition realignment. A person who calls themselves independent may still lean and behave like a partisan, while a partisan label does not predict every issue view or action.

observations.method: Published Pew subgroup comparisons from the 2026 NPORS; values describe affiliation within demographic groups and do not estimate causes of the differences.
observations.uncertainty: Group differences can reflect age, place, religion, income, education, race, gender, cohort, political events, and survey measurement together. They do not identify an individual-level mechanism.
observations.subgroup: Men and women; Black, Hispanic, and other race/ethnicity groups; adults with and without a college degree.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same subgroup can contain substantial internal variation, and group affiliation can move without corresponding movement in turnout, issue positions, or political action.

related_sources.claim: Pew's NPORS methodology and sample design provide context for the repeated cross-sectional estimates.

boundary: This record adds a current coalition-identity layer to the atlas. It shows how partisan affiliation and leaning differ across social groups and over time; it does not establish why people changed, how identity became a vote or policy demand, or whether a coalition shift will persist.
